title: 200 core words
hook: a whole book of people talking, and not one quotation mark: the tiny word that does the job
tomorrow: your right is to the work. so do results matter at all?

segments.voice: Yesterday, 200 core words met mamakah, mine: the word in the blind king's question that split a family. Today, words even smaller.

A page of Sanskrit has no quotation marks. None. Yet the Gita is people talking: Sanjaya to the king, Krishna to Arjuna, Arjuna back to Krishna. Text messages solve this with bubbles. Sanskrit had to solve it with a word. So how does a reader know where one voice stops and the next begins? The answer is a tiny word, and it's easy to read straight past.
screen: `NO QUOTATION MARKS.` → `A BOOK OF PEOPLE TALKING.` → `WHERE DOES A VOICE STOP?`

segments.voice: The word is iti. It means thus, and it works like a closing quotation mark. When someone finishes speaking, iti follows. The Gita's second chapter has a sharp example. Arjuna, standing between the armies, says to Krishna: na yotsya, I will not fight. Then iti. Then Sanjaya's voice again: and saying that, he fell silent. Without iti, a reader could take the silence as part of Arjuna's speech. With it, the voice has clearly changed. Iti can also name a word as a word: a teacher talking about the word dharma can follow it with iti, the way English uses quotation marks. And printed Gitas close each chapter with a line that begins iti: thus ends the chapter. Three more tiny words do the same quiet work. Ca, and. It comes after the word it adds, so pandavah ca means the sons of Pandu, and. Eva, just, indeed, leaning on the word before it to make it firm. Yesterday's chaiva is those two joined: ca plus eva. And na, not, the one inside Arjuna's refusal, and inside nasti and nasato. None of them is a teaching on its own. So why put words this small on a core list? Because they tell a reader how everything else fits: what's added, what's stressed, what's denied, and where someone stopped talking. Skip them, and a verse falls into a heap of nouns. Know them, and the sentence stands up. Small, and everywhere once you look.
screen: `ITI: THE CLOSING QUOTE MARK.` · `NA YOTSYA, ITI: HE FELL SILENT.` · `CA, EVA, NA.` · `HOW EVERYTHING ELSE FITS.` · then, large: `SMALL WORDS HOLD THE SENTENCE UP.`

segments.voice: Write down one short thing someone said to you this week, and after it, instead of a closing quotation mark, write the word iti; if nothing comes to mind, write Arjuna's na yotsya, then iti. Look at it for a moment: their words, then thus, the voice clearly closed. Then set the pen down and rest with the breath.
Two hundred core words. Today, the small ones that hold a sentence up: iti, thus; ca, and; eva, indeed; na, not.
The line for today: 200 core words, and the tiny ones show where a voice stops. Until tomorrow.

fork.setup: a friend reads Gita 2.9 aloud: 'na yotsya iti... and he fell silent.' she asks who said 'I will not fight.' what do you say?
options: Arjuna: iti closes his words, then Sanjaya says he fell silent.
Krishna: he refuses, and iti shows how angry he is.
Sanjaya: he's refusing to report the rest of the battle.
fork.reveal: iti closes Arjuna's refusal, na yotsya, I will not fight. the next words are Sanjaya's, telling the king that Arjuna fell silent.
